# Wiki Page State

What a page records that is not true yet sits on an axis chosen by what varies. This lookup holds the axes, the spellings each state takes, and the decisions-register rule built on axis 3.

**See also:** `wiki-authoring-spec` — for the readability rules and the list of every author-facing lookup.

## Page state axes

Some of what a page records is not true yet when the page is written: a decision that
has not been ratified, a cycle that has not been graded, an action item that has not
landed, a customer who has not approved the quote. A page type expresses that on the
axis chosen by **what varies** — the subject, one section, or the rows.

| Axis | It applies when | The mechanism |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1 — the subject has a lifecycle** | The page records one occurrence, commitment or artifact that itself moves through named states, and the whole page's meaning changes with the state | A page-level `status:` with a per-type vocabulary in `page-types.json` § `statusVocab`, plus `superseded-by` where supersession is real |
| **2 — a section is not yet due** | The page is complete and useful; one declared section fills at a named later event | The template's `Appends:` label declares the section and the event; the section reads `Pending: <event>.` until it arrives |
| **3 — a register of items with their own states** | State varies per row rather than per page | Per-row state stays in the body, and the template's `Columns:` label names the state columns an author may not trim — the general rule is in `wiki-template-labels` §Template labels |

The axes compose — `compliance-record` carries 1, 2 and `expires:` at once. A type that
carries none declares none; that is the rule producing an answer, not a gap.

**Axis 1 is not every page whose subject has states.** A page _about a class of thing_
that has states — `domain-object`, `system-entity`, `data-model-entity` — documents those
states as content in a `## Lifecycle` section, and the page itself is in no state. A page
recording _one_ occurrence or commitment is. An `adr` is proposed or accepted; a
`system-entity` describing an order's lifecycle is neither. Without this line every
reference page carrying a `## Lifecycle` section would wrongly take a `status:` field.

**Axis 2 is not bounded by cadence.** A `cadence: record` type is where later-filling
sections are most common, because a record's spine is authored once, but a living page can
hold a section that fills at a named event just as honestly — a launch plan's results
arrive when the launch does. What bounds `Pending:` is a _declaration_, not the cadence. A
section's `Pending:` is legal only in a section the template's `Appends:` line names, naming
an event that line declares. A cell's `Pending: <name>` sits outside any slot and has a
second bound: a row of the page's own `## Open questions` naming `<name>` (`wiki-cell-grammars` §Cell grammars).
Without its bound, a `Pending:` marker would be a sanctioned way to leave an
`error`-severity check suppressed indefinitely.

**Each state of a declared slot has one spelling.** `Pending: <event>.` while
the event is ahead; the filled content once it arrives; and `None. — <reason>.` when the
slot will never fill, naming why. A **bare** `None.` in a declared slot is an error,
because it cannot say whether the event happened and produced nothing or the author closed
the slot early. Outside a declared slot `None.` keeps its ordinary meaning from
`wiki-section-disposition` §Section disposition — considered, nothing to say — and is not read this way.

**`Pending:` is a value inside the Default form, not a fourth form.** Without it the grammar had two symbols for three states, and _not yet due_ had to be written `None.`, which says the author considered the section and had nothing to say. That is false, and it is the same defect the Default form's own rationale names (`wiki-section-disposition` §Section disposition). **The event token is the `Appends:` line's own words.** A template declares its slots as `<Section>[, <Section>] — <when>`, and `<when>` — the text after the dash, verbatim — is the string a page writes after `Pending:`. `pending-slot` compares the two, so an author needs no judgment about which fragment counts, and a template scaffolds the slot with that exact line rather than with empty structure: an empty table in a slot is neither content, `None.`, nor `Pending:`, and nothing can then tell a page awaiting its event from one that filled and was forgotten.

**A register declares its state columns.** The `Columns:` label is what stops a risk
register shipping without its Owner, Status or Residual risk column and still reading as
conformant. It is the general table-column declaration of `wiki-template-labels` §Template labels, not an
axis-3 mechanism of its own — a register is the case that motivated it, and field
inventories and scoring tables use the same label for rows that carry no state at all.

**Unresolved intent has one home per kind.** An **owned deferred decision** — something a
named person will settle by a named point — goes in `## Open questions`, which is a
register on the types that declare it. An **unowned research lead** — what a source raised
and did not answer — goes in `## Follow-up leads`, which is a bullet list and takes no
axis, because a lead nobody owns carries no state to track. A lead names what the source
leaves unanswered, or the detail it defers to a page it links, and never says that the wiki
lacks that page: the `sources/` folder is where that fact lives, and a lead that says so goes
false when the page is ingested. The rest of a `source-summary` page holds to the same: it
says what its snapshot leaves out, or that a figure is second-hand,
and never that the wiki has not ingested a source. A link to a page the wiki holds is a citation, which the
lint checks. The two headers are named apart for the
reason `wiki-authoring-spec` §Boundary statements gives: a reader moving between two page types should not meet
one header meaning two things. A type declaring neither holds unresolved intent inline, as
`concept` does, and says so.

Where a type's state vocabulary would depend on another of its fields — an
`operational-resource`'s states differ by whether its `kind` is a vendor or an environment
— it takes no `status:` today. `statusVocab` is keyed by type alone, deliberately, because
a union would let an `adr` declare `Expired`; a field-keyed vocabulary is mechanism that
one type does not justify. It becomes worth building when a second type wants the same
edge, and then keyed for both rather than bolted onto one.

### Decisions registers

A `## Decisions` register is the axis-3 table whose template's `Columns:` label declares
`Decision | State | Decided`. Each template says which calls its register takes and which
evidence a call cites; every such register then holds them by one rule:

- The register reads `None.` until the first call is recorded, and a call still under
  discussion sits in it as `proposed` rather than reading as made.
- A call is `proposed` until it cites a study or the designer signs it off; then it is
  `adopted`, and its Decision cell names what backs it — the study's
  `[[design:studies/<slug>]]` link, or `signed off by <designer>, <date>`. A comparison
  the call cites informs it but does not adopt it.
- The register holds the calls in force: when a call is replaced, rewrite its row to the
  new call, with `Decided` the date of the call in force — never keep the replaced call
  as a row.
- Where a call makes part of a live page stale — a cut acceptance criterion, a withdrawn
  commitment — name those pages in `invalidates:` and edit them in the same change; they
  cannot link back to the deciding page.
